## Problem and Context

Project DoLittle is an open-source effort by the CAIRN Institute to train a generative "audio language model" on humpback whale recordings \[1\]\[2\]. Raw audio from NOAA's SanctSound underwater microphones (hydrophones) is converted into discrete symbols (*tokens*) by a neural audio *codec*. The codec here is the Descript Audio Codec (DAC), which compresses sound into a short list of integers and can decode those integers back into sound \[5\]. A transformer, the network type behind text chatbots, learns to predict the next token, so it can continue a recorded song with new, whale-like audio \[2\]. The work serves bioacoustics researchers who want a humpback vocal model to probe, fine-tune, and generate from. Our capstone team is extending it with more data and with *metadata conditioning*: telling the model the station, year, and species of a recording.

This decision is about the **training pipeline**. DAC describes each \~11.6 ms audio frame with 9 tokens, one from each of 9 *codebooks*. The codebooks are stacked so that the first captures the coarse sound and each later one encodes what the earlier ones missed (*residual vector quantization*, RVQ). The current model *flattens* the 9 codebooks into one stream. That makes 775 tokens per second of audio, so a 13-second training window is 10,240 tokens \[1\]. All published training ran on one 16 GB consumer GPU (graphics processor) \[2\]. The code was shaped around that limit: batch size 1, memory-saving attention variants, and no support for more than one GPU \[1\].

Our team ran this code on Oregon State's College of Engineering high-performance computing (HPC) cluster for 6 days without completing one *epoch* (a full pass over the training data). The project partner advised us to look at open-source architectures that support parallel training. We need to decide whether to (a) extend the existing custom model so it trains in parallel and on shorter sequences, or (b) move to an established open-source framework, AudioCraft \[4\], which has these features built in. The choice is hard to reverse: it determines which codebase the team learns and maintains, how the data is fed in, and where the remaining HPC hours of the term are spent. **If we do nothing,** every experiment costs a week or more of GPU time, the metadata work cannot be evaluated this term, and we cannot iterate. We are currently moving forward with Option A,

### Option A: Parallelize the custom model

Keep the existing model and sequence format. Add PyTorch *DistributedDataParallel* (DDP), which runs one copy of the model per GPU, gives each copy different data, and averages the gradients after every step \[6\]. Each cluster node has 8 H100 GPUs \[7\], so assuming no overhead, training would see a 8-fold speed up. This would entail removing the leftovers of the 16 GB setup: raise the batch size, stop calling `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` after every optimizer step, and stop using half-overlapping training windows \[1\].

- **Benefits:** Small, well-documented change. Keeps the released checkpoints, configs, and evaluation scripts usable, so results stay directly comparable to the published baselines.  
- **Costs:** Sequences stay 9× longer than the audio's frame count, and attention cost grows with sequence length. Metadata conditioning still has to be added by hand. Would take a few days of engineering.  
- **Right choice when:** the goal is to reproduce or extend the published models exactly, or the team cannot afford to change the model's inputs this term.

### (optional) add the delay pattern

Another avenue than can be paralleized is our tokenization pattern. we have been investigating replacing flattening with MusicGen's *delay pattern* \[3\]. The model predicts all 9 codebooks at every step, but each codebook *k* is shifted back by *k*−1 steps, so the lower codebooks of a frame are still produced before the higher ones. 

![][image1]  
\[3\] 

MusicGen's authors showed that this allows all codebooks to be predicted in parallel, with only one autoregressive step per audio frame \[4\]. For our data, a 13-second window drops from about 10,240 positions to about 1,145. The pattern code can be adapted from AudioCraft's `codebooks_patterns.py` under its MIT license \[4\]. Metadata is added as reserved prefix tokens, in the same way the model already uses `SEP` boundary tokens \[1\].

- **Benefits:** Roughly 9× fewer positions per second of audio, on top of the multi-GPU speedup. Keeps our data loader and existing token files. The team keeps full control of the code.  
- **Costs:** About 1–2 weeks of engineering: a new input embedding (one table per codebook, summed), 9 output heads, and changes to sampling for generation. Old checkpoints can't be reused, so the published numbers become baselines rather than starting points. Bugs in our own port are a risk.  
- **Right choice when:** training speed is the binding constraint (it currently is), the team wants to keep the existing data pipeline, and the team can test its own implementation.

### Option B: Adopt AudioCraft (MusicGen language model)

Train with Meta's AudioCraft \[4\], which implements the delay pattern, multi-GPU training, Slurm (job scheduler) integration, and metadata conditioning. AudioCraft's documentation includes a training example using `dac_44khz` with 9 codebooks \[4\], which is the same codec and settings as our data.

- **Benefits:** A delay pattern already used for published models. Multi-GPU training with a single flag: `dora run -d` uses all available GPUs \[4\]. Ready-made conditioners for categorical metadata \[4\].  
- **Costs:** AudioCraft expects raw audio. Its token path is a training-only cache of fixed batches, and validation still expects audio \[4\]. Using our tokens needs a custom dataset and a patch to the training code (an estimated 150–250 lines). The framework is large, and its experiment mimanager (Dora) needs cluster-specific setup.  
- **Right choice when:** the team expects to rely on AudioCraft's conditioning and generation tools long-term, or our own delay-pattern port fails its correctness tests.

### Option C: Do nothing

Keep training the current configuration as it is.

- **Costs:** Based on the published run, one pass over the data takes weeks of single-GPU time (see Analysis), and each hyperparameter or metadata experiment takes the same. The cost is immediate: nothing new is learned this term.  
- **Right choice when:** the only goal is to finish one long reproduction run and nobody needs results quickly. (not our situation)  
- 

### Considered and set aside

- **Straight parallel.** Stacking the audiobooks instead of flattening natively without multiple refining passes causes artifacting, delay performs much better for O(num codebooks) additional runs\[3\]  
- **Fine-tuning VampNet/WhAM \[10\].** It starts from a pretrained model, but it has no metadata conditioning and predicts masked spans rather than the next token, so its results wouldn't be comparable to ours.  
- **A depth transformer (Moshi \[9\]).** It keeps the exact within-frame ordering but is more code than B. We'll revisit it if B's quality falls short.

## Analysis

**Where the time goes (our project evidence).** The 10k-context configuration builds training windows of 10,240 tokens that overlap by half (`stride = max_seq_len // 2` in `dataset.py`) and processes one window per step \[1\]. The dataset has about 488K token files of up to 30 seconds each \[1\]. At 775 tokens per second that is roughly 11B tokens, or about 2.2M overlapping windows per epoch before quality filtering (our arithmetic). The published 10k model ran 656,000 steps in about 132 hours \[2\], about 1.4 steps per second. At that rate one epoch would take about 18 days, Our 6-day result is consistent with the project partners training runs.

**Performance.**

- Option A's speedup comes from parallel data processing alone. With 8 GPUs we target close to 8× aggregate throughput (to be measured, not assumed).  
- Adding delay or pursuing Option B multiplies that by cutting sequence length about 9×. Attention cost growth is faster than linear, so the per-window saving is at least that large.  
- The quality cost of delay is small in the published evidence. In MusicGen's ablation on 30-second clips, flattening scored FAD 0.86 and delay 0.96, but flattening needed 6,000 steps against delay's 1,500 \[3\]. (FAD is Fréchet Audio Distance, where lower is closer to real audio, with 0 being exact match, up to positive infinity) The authors concluded that similar quality can be reached for a fraction of the cost with the delay approach \[3\].  
- **Uncertainty:** MusicGen used 4 codebooks and we have 9\. Other work notes that delay may not perform well with smaller models and 8/16 codebook configurations \[11\]. This is the main risk the verification plan has to catch.  
- For quality per token, flattening is the more expressive model. For quality per GPU-hour, our constraint, we expect delay to win, but this must be measured.

**Complexity.**

- A is the smallest change.  
- Adding a delay pattern touches the embedding, output, loss, and generation code, plus about 9 positions for each frame's index bookkeeping. Lots of manual work.  
- B swaps our \~2,700-line codebase \[1\] for a much larger framework and adds an adapter layer between our token files and AudioCraft.

**Maintainability.**

- In A the team owns code it already reads.  
- B inherits a mature design, but the AudioCraft repository's most recent commit was March 13, 2025, as of our clone on 2026-11-22 \[4\]. We would be adopting a framework with no recent upstream activity and maintaining our own patches against it.

**Security.** Low for all options. Checkpoint files can execute code when loaded, so we load only checkpoints we or the partner produced.

## Recommendation and Verification Plan

**Option A** is the obvious first step. It fixes the largest, most certain loss (one GPU of eight). The delay pattern then attacks the 9× sequence overhead, which no amount of hardware fixes. Compared with B, A keeps our token files and data loader, avoids depending on an inactive framework, and borrows AudioCraft's tested pattern logic under its license. B remains the fallback if A's checks fail.

**Milestone 1 (Option A):**

1. *Throughput:* record steps per second, audio-seconds trained per GPU-hour, and GPU utilization for the current code on one full H100. Then repeat on 8 GPUs with DDP. Acceptance: ≥ 6× aggregate audio-seconds per hour on 8 GPUs. (This is a target we set, not a published figure.)  
2. *Correctness:* run 1 GPU and 8 GPUs at the same global batch size from the same seed. Training loss should agree within run-to-run noise over the first 2,000 steps.  
3. *Allocation check:* each job logs `nvidia-smi` output showing a full 80 GB H100, not a MIG slice.

**Milestone 2 (delay pattern):** 4\. *Unit tests:*

- Applying the delay pattern to a token array and reversing it reproduces the input exactly.  
- A leakage test: changing tokens at step *s* must not change the model's outputs at any step before *s*.  
5. *Head-to-head comparison:* train the flattened (A) and delay models for equal GPU-hours on the same held-out split.  
   - Compare total negative log-likelihood per second of audio (*NLL*, the model's average surprise; lower is better), plus NLL for each codebook separately.  
   - Per-token perplexity is not comparable across sequence formats, so we don't use it here.  
   - Acceptance: delay pattern’s NLL per second is no worse than baseline A's at equal GPU-hours, and its coarse-codebook (1–3) NLL is no more than 5% worse than A's at equal tokens seen.  
6. *Generation:* run the repo's `analyze_generation_quality.py` and `grade_audio_quality.py` \[1\] on samples from both models, and do a blinded listening check against real clips.  
7. *Fallback trigger:* if test 4 fails after a reasonable debugging effort, or test 5 fails, re-run the comparison with Option B

Each milestone's results go in this RFC's revision log.

## Constraints

- **CAIRN code, Apache 2.0 \[1\].** Modifications are allowed. We keep the license and NOTICE and mark changed files.  
- **Project DoLittle dataset terms \[1\].** Publications must keep the terms file, acknowledge CAIRN, cite SanctSound \[12\], and not imply NOAA or Navy endorsement. This is a check before we publish anything. It rules out no option.  
- **AudioCraft \[4\].** The code is MIT, so Option B must keep its copyright notice on the copied pattern code; we add it to NOTICE. The MusicGen *weights* are CC-BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial). All our options train from scratch, so this matters only if someone later proposes starting from those weights.  
- **DAC \[5\].** MIT for code and weights, so no restriction.

## Delegation and Validation

- **Handed to AI (Claude, Anthropic):**  
    
  - Reading the CAIRN repository to find throughput bottlenecks.  
  - A literature and tool search for candidate architectures.  
  - Checking licenses.  
  - The epoch-time arithmetic.  
  - A first draft of this RFC.


- **Checks that made this reasonable:** every external claim has a reference a reviewer can open, and every repository claim points to a named file. The draft marked gaps as TODO instead of filling them in. The recommendation is tied to tests the team will run, not to the AI's prediction.  
    
- **Validated by hand before submission** (TODO: each team member confirms and initials the ones they checked):

  - MusicGen Table 4 values in \[3\].  
  - AudioCraft's license files and last-commit date \[4\].  
  - The cluster's GPU and MIG facts \[7\]  
  - Our own 6-day run's logs.


  We check these points by hand because the recommendation rests on them and switching sequence formats is hard to undo.

## Decision

Proposed, 2026-11-22. Pending team and project-partner review. Team Review Nov 23, project partner review Dec 3
